A 'fair value' is what analysts think a stock should be worth, like how much a toy is really worth versus its price tag. Palantir Technologies (PLTR) is a software company that helps big organizations, especially governments and large businesses, use artificial intelligence (AI) to make better decisions. Imagine you have a giant LEGO set — Palantir's tools help companies build with all the pieces faster and smarter. The stock recently closed at around $201, and even though it dipped about 4% on one recent trading day, it has rocketed up roughly 16-21% over the past month, beating most of its tech peers (IGV +6%, QQQ +2%) and the broader market (S&P 500 +2.06%). Its U.S. commercial business is exploding, with revenue jumping 149% year-over-year to $764 million in Q2 2026, customer count rising 35% to 653, and total contract value soaring 153% to $2.13 billion. Analysts expect Q3 2026 earnings of $0.42 per share (a 'share' is a tiny piece of ownership in a company) on $2.17 billion in revenue, both up roughly 84-100% from a year ago. However, the stock looks expensive compared to similar companies: its Forward P/E ratio (the price you pay today divided by expected future earnings — like paying $127 for $1 of future profit) sits at 127.52 versus an industry average of just 20.8, and its PEG ratio (which compares price to growth speed) of 2.3 is nearly double the industry average of 1.19, suggesting investors are paying a premium that could fall if growth slows.

Summary

Cameco (CCJ), a major uranium mining company, is currently trading at $81.47 per share but has fallen 36% from its all-time high and 26% over the last six months. Despite strong long-term tailwinds from AI data center demand and small modular reactor (SMR) interest, the company reported a disappointing Q2 2026 with Uranium segment EBITDA (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization—a measure of operating cash profit) dropping from CA$352M to CA$252M (a loss of CA$100M) and Westinghouse EBITDA swinging from a positive CA$126M to a negative CA$10M (a swing of CA$136M). Investors expect Q3 2026 earnings of $0.23 per share, a 360% jump from last year (EPS, or Earnings Per Share, is the slice of profit belonging to one share of stock), on revenue (total money earned from sales) of $494.94 million (up 10.91% YoY). However, the stock trades at a steep Forward P/E (Price-to-Earnings ratio: how many dollars you pay for each dollar of profit—lower is usually cheaper) of 80.77 versus an industry average of 17.7, suggesting it is expensive relative to peers, even though its PEG ratio (a P/E that accounts for growth—closer to 1 is fairer) of 1.76 is slightly below the industry average of 2.02. Upcoming catalysts include the Westinghouse IPO (Initial Public Offering—selling shares to the public for the first time), whose technology powers 57% of the world's 417 operating reactors. Cameco Corporation (CCJ), one of the world's largest uranium producers with 49% ownership of Westinghouse, is a Canadian nuclear fuel company that has seen its stock retreat from a 52-week high of $135.24 to around $85-88 recently—a decline of roughly 5.58% over the past month and 4.44% over the past year, with a market capitalization of approximately $38.35 billion. The company's Q2 2026 results were disappointing, with uranium segment earnings falling nearly 40% year-over-year despite an 18% increase in average realized uranium prices to US$67.79 per pound; adjusted EPS (earnings per share—meaning the slice of profit belonging to one single share of the company, like cutting a pizza into tiny pieces) came in at just C$0.18, well below the C$0.38 estimate, while adjusted EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization—a way to measure how much cash a business makes from its main work before paying certain bills) reached roughly $279 million. Long-term uranium demand looks strong, with UxC estimating utilities need about 3.1 billion pounds of uncovered uranium through 2045 versus only 589 million pounds placed under contract over the past five years, and Cameco has contracts for over 28 million pounds of annual deliveries through 2030, including a new 9-year, ~$2.6 billion India supply agreement. Despite operational disruptions from Saskatchewan flooding and a two-week Cigar Lake production halt, the company maintained its 2026 production guidance of 19.5–21.5 million pounds and holds a solid balance sheet with ~$784 million in cash against $713 million in debt plus an undrawn $713 million credit facility. The company generates about CA$2.9 billion from uranium, CA$551 million from fuel services, and CA$3.4 billion from its Westinghouse segment. The company owns 49% of Westinghouse (a nuclear reactor builder), which is about to go public and could be worth CA$24 billion to Cameco, a massive return on its $2.1 billion original investment. Cameco recently missed its quarterly earnings significantly, with Q2 EPS (earnings per share, meaning the company's profit divided by total shares - basically how much money each share earned) coming in at C$0.18 versus the C$0.38 analysts expected, and net earnings (the actual money the company keeps after paying all bills) dropped 92% year-over-year to just C$25 million. Despite this, Wall Street analysts remain bullish with 11 buys, 8 outperforms, and only 2 holds, with an average price target of C$179 (47% above current levels) and some firms like Jefferies setting even higher C$190 targets. The company's valuation model suggests a target of $122 (40% upside) assuming operating margins (the percentage of sales left as profit) nearly double to 30% by 2028, but this is heavily dependent on contract pricing improvements as old uranium contracts roll off. Cameco (CCJ) is the world's second-largest uranium miner (about 15% of global production in 2025) and co-owns 49% of Westinghouse Electric. Recently, big news dropped: the US and South Korea announced a framework where Korea would invest US$120 billion to help build up to 8 nuclear reactors in the US (6 Westinghouse AP1000s and up to 2 Korean APR1400s), with each APR1400 reactor expected to bring ~US$2 billion in value to Westinghouse. Westinghouse is also reportedly aiming for a US IPO valued above US$50 billion, which could make Cameco's 49% stake worth over US$24.5 billion (about 64% of Cameco's ~US$38.3B market cap). However, the stock has pulled back from its January 28, 2026 record high of $134.09/share to around $87-88, with shares losing 15.43% recently and dropping 2.95% in a recent session. Cameco's Q2 results disappointed, with adjusted EPS of just C$0.18 versus the C$0.38 analysts expected (this means earnings per share—how much profit the company made for each piece of its stock—came in at less than half what people predicted), and its share of Westinghouse adjusted EBITDA dropped from C$352M to C$163M year-over-year. Uranium prices have recovered from $18/lb in Nov 2016 to $89.68/lb recently, but Cameco trades at a very expensive Forward P/E of 75.77 (a P/E ratio is like a price tag—the number tells you how many dollars investors are willing to pay for every dollar of profit the company makes; the higher it is, the more expensive the stock looks) compared to the industry average of 17.44. Cameco (CCJ) is one of the world's largest uranium miners with significant exposure across the nuclear fuel value chain, including a 49% stake in Westinghouse Electric worth potentially $24.5 billion if Westinghouse IPOs at a $50 billion valuation, compared to Cameco's $2.1 billion original investment and current $2.9 billion carrying value. The company's earnings per share (EPS - which is the portion of company profit divided by each share of stock, like splitting a pizza among shareholders) is projected to surge 420% to $0.26 for the upcoming quarter, with revenue expected at $494.94 million (a 10.91% increase year-over-year). However, Cameco's stock has underperformed recently, declining 1.27% on the most recent trading day to $91.62 and falling 2.92% over the past month, lagging both the broader market (S&P 500) and the Oils-Energy sector. The stock trades at a high Forward P/E ratio (price-to-earnings, which means how many dollars you pay for each dollar of company profit - lower is generally cheaper) of 72.96, which is roughly 4x the industry average of 17.89, suggesting investors are paying a premium for future growth. Cameco benefits from exceptionally low production costs of approximately $21.72 to $23.94 per pound of uranium, plus exposure to the global nuclear renaissance, including a landmark $80 billion U.S. government deal and $17.5 billion DOE loan commitment to Westinghouse to build 10 AP1000 reactors. The Zacks Rank of #3 (Hold) and Industry Rank of 149 (bottom 40%) suggest analyst caution, while the PEG ratio (a number that compares the P/E to the company's growth rate - lower than P/E means the growth may justify the price) of 1.59 is actually below the industry's 2.22, indicating reasonable growth-adjusted valuation.

In Q2, the company reported revenues of $176.1 million, up 14% year-on-year, beating analyst expectations by 16.4%. Centrus Energy (NYSE: LEU), a nuclear fuel supplier, saw its stock jump 7.1% (closing up 6.6% at $148.40) after announcing a definitive multi-year High-Assay Low-Enriched Uranium (HALEU) supply agreement with Antares Nuclear, with deliveries set to commence before 2030. This positive news comes against a backdrop of significant challenges: the stock is down 45.3% year-to-date and trading 65.8% below its 52-week high of $436 reached in October 2025. Just seven days before this rally, the stock dropped 8.6% following the pricing of a $500 million underwritten public offering consisting of 500,000 Class A shares, pre-funded warrants for 2,005,513 shares, and common warrants for up to 6,992,382 additional shares — meaning 'dilution' (giving out new pieces of ownership paper that could turn into real shares), which spreads the company's value across more owners and shrinks each owner's slice. The stock is highly volatile with 86 moves greater than 5% over the past year. Despite recent struggles, long-term holders who invested $1,000 five years ago would now have $4,052, a 305% gain. Centrus operates the only licensed HALEU production facility in the western world at its American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio, and is pursuing a multi-billion-dollar expansion. Centrus Energy (LEU), a company that enriches uranium for nuclear fuel, has reported mixed recent results with significant long-term potential but concerning near-term trends. In Q2 2026, revenue grew 14% to $176.1 million, beating expectations of $147 million, with the Low-Enriched Uranium (LEU) segment rising 22% to $153.4 million and uranium sales jumping to $53.4 million from zero a year earlier. However, EPS (earnings per share - the profit divided by total shares, so what each share 'owns' of the company's profit) dropped 51.6% to 77 cents, gross margin (the percentage of revenue left after paying for the stuff the company sells) fell from 34.9% to 28.3%, and operating income plunged 69% to $10.4 million. Despite a strong $4.5 billion backlog (orders already promised for delivery through 2040) and major wins including a $900 million DOE task order and potential military contracts, the stock trades at a very high P/E ratio (price-to-earnings - how many dollars investors pay for each dollar of profit) of 72.9x versus an industry average of 13x. The stock has declined 34.99% YTD (year-to-date), underperformed peers with a -4.4% one-year return, but still boasts a 5-year return of approximately 5.7x. Analysts see a fair value of $190 (about 6.8% upside from the $177.14 current price), though valuation models flag the stock as expensive. Centrus Energy (LEU) reported strong Q2 2026 results with revenue of $176.1 million, up 14% year-over-year, and adjusted net income of $38.7 million (or $1.77 per diluted share, which means the company's profit divided by all its shares). Its LEU segment grew 22% to $153.4 million. The company has a massive $4.5 billion commercial backlog stretching to 2040, including $3.7 billion in LEU. Centrus secured a $900 million HALEU task order from the Department of Energy (HALEU is a special type of nuclear fuel), plus new deals with Oklo and X-energy, and announced a multi-billion dollar Piketon, Ohio expansion expected to create about 1,000 construction jobs and 300 permanent roles. Management maintained 2026 revenue guidance of $450–$500 million. However, analyst sentiment turned cautious: Simply Wall St's modeled fair value dropped from $269.38 to $257.47, net profit margin (the percentage of revenue kept as profit) fell from 14.45% to 7.19%, and forward P/E (a ratio comparing share price to expected future earnings—higher means investors pay more for each dollar of profit) ballooned from 126.1x to 222.1x, with UBS, BofA, JPMorgan and Roth Capital all cutting price targets.

Summary

Berkshire Hathaway (BRK-B), the trillion-dollar conglomerate that transitioned leadership from Warren Buffett to Greg Abel on December 31, is undergoing a notable strategic shift. Approximately 45% of its $356 billion investment portfolio (about $160.6 billion) remains concentrated in just three 'undeniable winners': Apple (AAPL), American Express (AXP), and Alphabet (GOOGL/GOOG). Apple was trimmed heavily by Buffett—he dumped 75% of Berkshire's Apple stake over nine quarters before retiring—though Abel views Apple as a long-term compounder. On the operating side, Berkshire is now the nation's 4th-largest homebuilder after a $6.8 billion acquisition of Taylor Morrison (combined with its existing Clayton Homes unit), a July acquisition of South Carolina builder McGuinn, and a near-doubling of its stake in Lennar to 11% (plus smaller stakes in NVR and D.R. Horton). The downside is a deteriorating housing market: existing-home sales have hovered around 4 million annually since 2022, well below the pre-pandemic average of 5.5 million, with mortgage rates above 7% and a 'lock-in effect' freezing inventory. Analyst projections call for 2029 revenue of $448.5 billion (5.3% annual growth) but earnings falling to $53.1 billion—a decline of $32.7 billion from the current $85.8 billion earnings base, signaling expected pressure on profitability. 'Revenue' is just the total money a company brings in from selling stuff, and 'earnings' is what's left after paying all the bills—basically the company's profit. The difference between a stock's earnings today and tomorrow is what investors care about most. Berkshire Hathaway (BRK-B) is undergoing a major leadership transition, with Greg Abel now serving as CEO after Warren Buffett's legendary tenure, during which BRK delivered an annualized return of 19.7% from 1965 through 2025, vastly outperforming the S&P 500's 10.5% average yearly return. Under Abel, Berkshire is pivoting aggressively toward technology, with tech now comprising approximately 33% of equity holdings — a dramatic shift from Buffett's historically tech-averse stance. Key new positions include Alphabet (GOOGL), now the third-largest holding at 3.4% of market cap with shares up 49% over the past 12 months and trading at a forward P/E ratio (a measure comparing the stock price to expected future earnings — think of it as 'how many dollars you pay for each dollar of profit') of 22.8. Berkshire also invested an additional $330M into Italian tech conglomerate Bending Spoons, bringing total commitment to ~$930M for a 4% stake, negotiated at a 13% private placement discount at $33/share (with shares subsequently surging 41%+). Bending Spoons guides for 113% YoY revenue growth, ~$2.8B full-year 2026 revenue, ~$1.5B adjusted operating income (profit from core business before interest and taxes), $453M TTM free cash flow (cash left after paying bills and investing), and ~55% projected annual earnings growth over five years. Berkshire Hathaway (ticker BRK-B) just made another bet on Italian tech company Bending Spoons (BSP), putting in another $330 million at $33 per share in a private placement (a deal where a company sells new shares directly to one buyer, not on the open stock market). This adds to the $600 million Berkshire already invested at Bending Spoons' July 2026 IPO (when a company first sells shares to the public), for a total commitment of around $930 million, giving Berkshire a 4% ownership stake. BRK-B stock barely reacted, rising just 1.11% to $526.35, because $330 million is tiny compared to Berkshire's massive $380 billion cash pile (the total money Berkshire has saved up). So far in 2026, BRK-B has gained only about 3%, lagging behind the S&P 500 (a group of 500 of America's biggest companies used as a yardstick) which gained about 14%. However, history is on Berkshire's side: since 1965, Berkshire's stock has beaten the S&P 500 in 11 out of 13 years when the market went down, earning a compounded annual gain (the average yearly growth if profits were reinvested each year) of 19.7% versus 10.5% for the S&P 500. Berkshire Hathaway (BRK-B) made headlines by investing an additional $330 million in Bending Spoons (BSP), an Italian technology company, through a private placement of 10 million shares at $33 each, bringing Berkshire's total investment to approximately $930 million and its ownership stake to about 4%. This follows a $600 million investment during BSP's July IPO, when shares closed at $40.50 on debut day. The news caused Bending Spoons stock to surge roughly 40% in a single trading session, pushing the year-to-date gain to approximately 63% and trading around $54 per share. Bending Spoons operates as a 'technology-focused Berkshire Hathaway,' acquiring software and digital media brands like AOL, Evernote, Vimeo, Eventbrite, and Airtable—mirroring Buffett's classic buy-and-hold philosophy but in the tech space. While this signals Berkshire's continued aggressive capital deployment under new leadership, critics note BSP trades at a pricey forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of about 27x (meaning investors pay $27 for every $1 of future yearly profit, which is considered expensive), and Wall Street's mean price target of $46 suggests potential downside from current levels. The move represents a notable strategic shift, as BSP is described as 'a curveball'—a pricey growth equity rather than the value stocks Berkshire traditionally favors. Berkshire Hathaway (BRK-B) is undergoing a notable strategic transformation under new CEO Greg Abel, following Warren Buffett's departure as CEO on January 1 and as chairman on September 18 at age 96. The conglomerate's stock is up 5.30% year-to-date, trading near $522 and approaching its all-time high of $540 set in May 2025. Berkshire holds a massive $1.263 trillion in total assets as of June, with technology now its largest sector holding at 33.2% of the portfolio (worth ~$119.6 billion), reflecting a significant pivot from Buffett's historically tech-averse approach. The company has made major new investments including a $37.4 billion position in Alphabet (third-largest holding, ~10% of the $358 billion stock portfolio) and $930 million total in Italian tech company Bending Spoons (4% stake). With more than $370 billion in cash and U.S. Treasury holdings, Berkshire has substantial firepower for further acquisitions, including the recently completed $6.8 billion acquisition of Taylor Morrison Home Corp. The insurance segment, contributing approximately one-fourth of total revenues, continues to provide a stable earnings foundation through disciplined underwriting (which means carefully deciding which risks to insure and charging appropriate prices) and a low-cost insurance float (the pool of premium money collected before claims are paid out, which Berkshire invests).

Summary

ASML, a company that makes special machines used to build computer chips (especially the most advanced AI chips), had an amazing third quarter in 2026. They earned a record €11.7 billion in sales (that's money customers paid them), which was at the high end of what they expected. Their 'gross margin' (the money they keep after paying to build their products, like the difference between selling a lemonade for $1 and the $0.30 it cost to make) was a huge 57.5%—meaning they kept €0.575 of every euro earned. Over the last 12 months, they made €10.6 billion in profit (net income—money left after ALL bills are paid), up 12.4% from the year before. Their 'earnings per share' or EPS (imagine a pizza split into pieces—EPS is how big each shareholder's slice of the profit pie is) was €27.57, up 13.7%. But here's the tricky part: the stock is expensive! It trades at a 'P/E ratio' (price-to-earnings—a way to measure if a stock is pricey by comparing its price to its profits, like comparing how many pizzas you have to give up to buy one) of 52.9x, which is way above what some experts think it's worth (€955.78 per share based on future cash). Customers are now ordering machines as far ahead as 2029 and 2030, and ASML can't build enough machines to keep up with demand—a great problem to have! ASML Holding N.V., the Dutch maker of advanced chipmaking machines (especially EUV lithography tools that etch tiny patterns on silicon chips), reported record Q3 2026 sales of €11.66 billion (about $11.66 billion), which slightly missed analyst expectations of €11.72 billion but jumped 55.2% from a year earlier. Gross margin (the share of sales left after just the cost of making the product) expanded to 57.5% from 54% last quarter, showing the company is becoming more efficient. Total system sales were €8.4 billion, split between €4.1 billion from EUV (extreme ultraviolet) systems (including one High-NA EUV machine, which is the most advanced type) and €4.3 billion from non-EUV systems, with logic chips at 54% and memory chips at 46% of system sales. ASML, the world's most important maker of lithography machines (specialized equipment that etches tiny circuit patterns onto silicon chips, essentially the 'printing press' for advanced semiconductors), reported very strong earnings recently, but its U.S.-listed stock actually fell despite the good news. The company raised its sales guidance (meaning it told Wall Street it expects to earn more money than it previously predicted) because it literally cannot keep up with how many machines customers want to buy. ASML said its current plans won't let it build enough machines to meet all the orders it has for 2027 and 2028, and is now looking at ways to build even MORE machines than the 30% increase in capacity it had already announced for 2028. This demand is being driven by 'soaring' (very rapidly growing) spending on AI chips. Think of it like a toy company that sells the most popular toy in the world — they could sell way more toys, but they can't build their factories fast enough to make enough toys. So even though business is amazing, the stock price dropped because of bigger worries about the whole 'chip stock' group, which fell for 7 days in a row — their longest losing streak since May 2025. Other companies in ASML's orbit (like Ichor Holdings at $2 billion market cap and Marketech International at NT$141.2 billion) also stand to benefit from this AI spending wave.

Separately, Intel is embroiled in a U.S. Supreme Court case regarding its employee retirement plan, where critics allege excessive fees and questionable investment structures (like hiding a private equity/hedge fund inside a master trust — basically stuffing exotic, high-cost investments into the retirement savings account that workers rely on for their future). The chipmaker earned $0.42 per share on an adjusted basis (meaning what each tiny slice of the company earned after ignoring one-time costs), more than double its own guidance of $0.20 and reversing a $0.10 loss from a year ago. However, the foundry business (Intel's factory-building arm) posted a massive $2.1 billion operating loss despite 31% revenue growth, signaling heavy spending. JPMorgan Chase (JPM), the world's largest bank by market capitalization, is making strategic moves around artificial intelligence while managing significant risks. CEO Jamie Dimon has publicly embraced AI internally—launching a pilot for 'Smart Cash,' an AI tool designed to predict customers' cash flow (the money coming in and going out of their bank account) and move funds to maximize yield (earn more interest)—but has drawn a firm line against allowing 'rogue' AI agents (outside computer programs that act on their own) from third parties to access customer accounts, citing too much risk for clients and the bank. The bank's Q3 earnings call highlighted this dual approach. On the consumer protection front, Chase hosted a National Cybersecurity Awareness Month event streamed to approximately 700 branches nationwide, serving over 1 million customers through financial health initiatives and running more than 1,000 fraud-prevention workshops each year. Lightbridge Corporation (NASDAQ: LTBR) is an advanced nuclear fuel technology company that ended Q1 2026 with approximately $215.7 million in cash, raised an additional $18.6 million through its ATM (At-The-Market, a way companies can sell shares gradually to investors to raise money) program during the quarter, but reported a wider net loss of $6.3 million due to increased R&D (Research & Development, meaning money spent on creating new products and testing them) and stock-based compensation (paying employees partly with company shares instead of just salary). The company secured major patent allowances across three jurisdictions—the United States, Canada, and the European Patent Office (covering 39 European contracting states)—strengthening intellectual property protection for its helically twisted/multi-lobed fuel designs and multi-zone fuel elements. Lightbridge also expanded operational capabilities to over 24 in-house engineers and secured partnerships including a multi-phase thermal-hydraulic testing contract with Stern Laboratories and selection to a $6 million DOE (U.S. Department of Energy)-funded Industry Advisory Board at Penn State. The company's flagship Lightbridge Fuel™ technology promises power uprates (boosting how much electricity a reactor can produce) of up to 30% for new-build water-cooled reactors and 20%+ for existing light-water reactors (the most common type of nuclear reactor that uses regular water to cool the reactor core), while operating approximately 1,000°C cooler than alternatives. Net loss (when a company spends more money than it earns) widened, reflecting accelerated investment rather than operational deterioration, and the substantial cash reserve provides roughly 8+ years of runway at current burn rates.

Qualcomm (QCOM) is undergoing a major business transformation, shifting from smartphone dependency toward diversified revenue streams. In its latest quarter, the company reported $9.9 billion in revenue (which is the total money the company brought in from selling things) and $2.21 per share in earnings (EPS means earnings per share, which is how much profit the company made for each piece of stock an investor owns). Automotive revenue hit a record $1.6 billion, up 61% year-over-year, marking 23 consecutive quarters of double-digit growth. The company signed a landmark deal with Amazon for up to $60 billion in payments (that's how much money Amazon agreed to potentially spend on Qualcomm chips) tied to actual chip purchases, with 3.75 million shares already vested (meaning Amazon earned those shares for keeping its promise to buy). Non-handset revenue is projected to accelerate from 24% growth in fiscal 2026 to over 60% in fiscal 2027, with a $40 billion revenue target by fiscal 2029. Despite these positives, the stock at $176 trades at a discount to its 52-week high of $260, has underperformed the industry (8.5% vs 28.8% over the past year), and faces an unresolved licensing dispute with Arm that ended in a hung jury.

EPS (earnings per share - how much money the company made for each piece of its stock) soared from $2.92 to $4.60, beating the $4.46 estimate, meaning each share of TSMC made much more profit than people thought it would. The company's gross margin (the percentage of money left after paying to make its products) expanded from 59.5% to 66.4%, and operating margin (money left after running the business) grew from 50.6% to 58.7%, showing TSMC can charge more for its chips. Cutting-edge 3nm chips (the smallest, most advanced chip technology - 'nm' means nanometers, super tiny measurements) became its biggest revenue source at 33%, while high-performance computing (HPC) chips mostly used for AI (artificial intelligence - computer brains that can learn) made up 68% of sales. Despite these exceptional results and positive guidance for the current quarter, TSM stock fell because the entire AI sector was getting scared about things like rising interest rates (the cost of borrowing money), competition from China, and worries about risky 'circular financing deals' (when companies essentially fund their own customers). Separately, Taiwan announced plans to develop industrial parks in the US, starting with a $4 billion Texas complex, to support TSMC's supply chain, with TSMC having pledged $265 billion for U.S. expansion. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSM), the world's largest contract chip manufacturer, reported its sixth consecutive quarter of record profits for Q3 2026, showcasing explosive growth driven by AI chip demand. Profitability remained elite, with gross margin (the percentage of revenue left after subtracting the direct cost of making chips) at 66.4%, operating margin (what's left after subtracting all operating expenses, not just production costs) at 58.7%, EPS (earnings per share, meaning the company's profit divided by the number of shares, expressed in Taiwan dollars) of TWD 29.43, and ROE (return on equity, which measures how much profit the company generates for every dollar shareholders have invested) of 45.5%. Advanced nodes (the most tiny, powerful chip manufacturing sizes, 7nm and below) drove 79% of wafer revenue, with 2nm already contributing 8% despite some near-term margin dilution. Summary

Microsoft (MSFT) recently announced two significant developments: the completion of pre-training for MAI-Base-2, a new AI model claiming to outperform OpenAI's GPT-5.6 using only 25% of the computing power, and a 20-year, 1,100 MW power agreement with NiSource for a northwest Indiana data center campus beginning in 2028. MAI-Base-2 is a mixture-of-experts model with 80 billion active parameters and 2.8 trillion total parameters, trained on 16,000 GB200 chips over 38 days, reportedly achieving 4-12x better pre-training efficiency than DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base. Microsoft's market cap stands at $4.01 trillion, with a $135 billion OpenAI stake supporting Azure revenue, and CFO Amy Hood highlighted margin improvement opportunities from this dual strategy. The stock showed modest movement—rising 1.08% to $539.44 on October 15 before dipping 0.47% to $536.88 after hours—indicating the market is cautiously awaiting concrete proof. Additionally, MSFT shares gained 0.32% in premarket trading following the NiSource deal announcement. Microsoft (MSFT) reported exceptional quarterly results with Azure cloud revenue exceeding $100 billion for fiscal year 2026 and Q4 Azure growth reaching 43%, demonstrating strong momentum in its AI and cloud business. The company has accumulated $678 billion in commercial cloud remaining performance obligations (which means customers have promised to pay Microsoft this much money in the future for cloud services they already signed up for - think of it like a giant stack of IOUs from customers). Microsoft plans massive capital expenditures (spending money to build things like data centers) of $175-190 billion in 2026, primarily for AI infrastructure. The company is making a strategic shift to use its own custom-designed Maia AI chips at massive scale (multi-gigawatt means enough electricity to power a large city) starting next year, reducing reliance on Nvidia. However, Microsoft faces significant headwinds including UK regulatory scrutiny of its business software bundling practices (where they sell multiple programs together like Word, Excel, and Teams as a package), potential Democratic congressional investigations after midterm elections, and execution risks if AI demand doesn't keep pace with the massive infrastructure spending. Microsoft (MSFT) is experiencing strong bullish momentum heading into its October 28 earnings report, driven primarily by accelerating AI-related business across Azure cloud services, enterprise AI orchestration, and proprietary model development. UBS has raised its price target by 28.6% from $525 to $675, citing AI demand supporting a valuation of 23x estimated 2027 adjusted earnings (meaning investors pay $23 for every $1 of expected earnings — a way to measure if a stock is expensive or cheap). Azure revenue is expected to grow 47% for the September quarter, representing a potential 2-percentage-point beat versus expectations. Microsoft's stock has rallied 39% since its June-quarter results. A Morgan Stanley CIO survey found Microsoft leads in AI orchestration with 20% share vs. LLM providers at 17%, Google at 5%, and Amazon at 4%. Additionally, 30% of CIOs named Microsoft as the vendor most likely to capture the biggest share of generative AI spending in 2026 (up from 27% the prior quarter). Microsoft also announced MAI-Base-2, a 2.8 trillion-parameter AI model that is 4.2 to 12.3 times more compute-efficient than DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base, demonstrating significant efficiency gains. The broader Pegasus Program continues to onboard startups like Tucuvi, which operates across 80+ health settings and 50+ workflow types, expanding Microsoft's healthcare AI ecosystem. Microsoft (MSFT) is experiencing a complex set of dynamics heading into earnings, with significant analyst optimism tempered by execution and valuation concerns. However, MSFT has underperformed the broader market, gaining only 4% versus the S&P 500's 16% over the past year, with the latest quarter showing $90 billion in revenue (up only 18%) and diluted EPS (earnings per share — basically the company's profit divided among all its shares) of $4.81 (up 32%). Heavy capital expenditure (capex — money the company spends on big things like buildings and equipment) of $115.95 billion in fiscal 2026, expected to reach $175 billion in fiscal 2027, has pressured free cash flow (the cash left over after paying for big investments — down 23.19% to $19.64 billion in the June quarter), leading to reported 20% cost-cutting demands in Azure (which Microsoft denied). With a market cap hovering between $3.9–$3.96 trillion, Microsoft faces a 'legacy business drag' as competitors like Anthropic grow at 50% quarter-over-quarter with a potential $2 trillion IPO valuation. Microsoft (MSFT) is a massive tech company now worth about $4 trillion, with its stock bouncing back strong after a scare. The stock price climbed from $512.80 on October 1 to $533.69 by October 14, even after briefly dipping to $522.61 on October 8 when bad news hit. From June 30 to early October, the stock jumped nearly 39%, showing investors really like Microsoft. The company earned $17.95 per share in fiscal year 2026 (EPS, or earnings per share, means how much profit the company made for each tiny piece of its stock), and analysts think it will grow to $19.76 next year, about 14% more. Microsoft is selling a new product bundle called E7 for $99 per user per month, which is helping its Microsoft 365 cloud business grow 14% even though it only added 6% more customers—meaning each customer is paying Microsoft more money.
